title: Sorting
summary: Pick a sort by stability, worst-case bound, and whether input is almost ordered.

parts.rule: Any general comparison sort needs at least about n log n comparisons in the worst case. Mergesort keeps that bound and preserves equal-key order. Heapsort also guarantees n log n with little extra memory. Quicksort is fast on average yet can degrade to quadratic without a careful pivot plan. Counting and radix methods beat n log n when keys are integers from a limited range. Stability means equal keys keep their original relative order.
parts.why: Telling an interviewer to "just sort" is incomplete when they ask which algorithm and why. Stability matters for multi-key sorts; worst-case matters on adversarial input; nearly sorted data can make a simple insertion pass attractive. Naming the bound and the property shows judgment rather than habit.
parts.example: Mergesort on [3, 1, 3, 2]: split into [3,1] and [3,2]; sort into [1,3] and [2,3]; merge by comparing heads — take 1, then 2, then the 3 from the left half (stability), then the remaining 3, yielding [1,2,3,3]. Quicksort with pivot 2 on [3,1,3,2] partitions into [1], the pivot 2, and [3,3], then recurses. Counting sort on grades [2,1,2,0] with values in 0..2 builds counts [1,1,2], turns them into placement indexes, and writes output [0,1,2,2] in time linear in n plus the range. Prefer counting when the range is tiny; prefer mergesort when stability and a hard n log n ceiling both matter.
parts.use: Call a library sort unless the prompt forbids it, and still name its expected bound. Choose mergesort when stability and worst-case n log n both matter. Choose counting or radix for small-range integers. Remember that sorting unlocks two-pointer scans and binary search afterward.
parts.refuse: Do not ship quicksort without a pivot strategy if worst-case behavior is under discussion. Do not apply plain counting sort to arbitrary strings without a radix plan. Do not pick an unstable sort when equal keys carry payload order that must survive. Do not sort at all when a single frequency pass already answers the question.

body:
Rule. Any general comparison sort needs at least about n log n comparisons in the worst case. Mergesort keeps that bound and preserves equal-key order. Heapsort also guarantees n log n with little extra memory. Quicksort is fast on average yet can degrade to quadratic without a careful pivot plan. Counting and radix methods beat n log n when keys are integers from a limited range. Stability means equal keys keep their original relative order.

Why it matters. Telling an interviewer to "just sort" is incomplete when they ask which algorithm and why. Stability matters for multi-key sorts; worst-case matters on adversarial input; nearly sorted data can make a simple insertion pass attractive. Naming the bound and the property shows judgment rather than habit.

Worked example. Mergesort on [3, 1, 3, 2]: split into [3,1] and [3,2]; sort into [1,3] and [2,3]; merge by comparing heads — take 1, then 2, then the 3 from the left half (stability), then the remaining 3, yielding [1,2,3,3]. Quicksort with pivot 2 on [3,1,3,2] partitions into [1], the pivot 2, and [3,3], then recurses. Counting sort on grades [2,1,2,0] with values in 0..2 builds counts [1,1,2], turns them into placement indexes, and writes output [0,1,2,2] in time linear in n plus the range. Prefer counting when the range is tiny; prefer mergesort when stability and a hard n log n ceiling both matter.

When to use. Call a library sort unless the prompt forbids it, and still name its expected bound. Choose mergesort when stability and worst-case n log n both matter. Choose counting or radix for small-range integers. Remember that sorting unlocks two-pointer scans and binary search afterward.

When to refuse. Do not ship quicksort without a pivot strategy if worst-case behavior is under discussion. Do not apply plain counting sort to arbitrary strings without a radix plan. Do not pick an unstable sort when equal keys carry payload order that must survive. Do not sort at all when a single frequency pass already answers the question.
